question.text: The Sahyadri Stat-Arb Fund has a master in India with total NAV INR 400 crore across 40,00,000 units (NAV Rs. 1,000). An offshore feeder (Mauritius) holds 5,00,000 master units. Management fee at master: 2% p.a., accrued daily, shown via master NAV. Feeder charges a nominal USD 1,000 admin fee only. What is the feeder's effective economic exposure at a given day's NAV strike of Rs. 1,020?

answer.text: INR 50 crore (5,00,000 units × Rs. 1,000 at old NAV)
INR 51 crore (5,00,000 units × Rs. 1,020 current NAV)
INR 50 crore less the 2% master management fee deducted at feeder level
USD 1,000 only (the feeder's nominal admin fee)

explanation.text: The Logic: Feeder holds 5,00,000 units in the master. Current NAV is Rs. 1,020 — the 2% management fee is already reflected in the master NAV (via daily accrual), NOT separately at feeder. Feeder's economic exposure = 5,00,000 x 1,020 = INR 51 crore. The USD 1,000 symbolic fee at feeder is trivial and not the economic exposure. The Trap: Option A uses stale NAV. Option C double-counts the management fee (already in the master NAV). Option D confuses the fee with the exposure. Cross-Exam Context: Master-feeder NAV math is consistent across XIX-C/D/E. Manager's Pro-Tip: In master-feeder, always strike the master NAV first, then compute feeder NAV as (feeder's master-unit-count x master NAV) less feeder-level expenses. Feeder expenses should be immaterial — if they aren't, re-negotiate or restructure.
